For most of the twentieth century, neuroscientists regarded a stored memory as something akin to an inscription in stone. Once the brain had turned a fragile new experience into a durable trace, the trace was presumed to be essentially (A) ____, safe from any later change. This orthodoxy began to crumble in 2000 with a study of laboratory rats: after a simple reminder had reactivated a fear memory, the memory became labile again for a time. A drug blocking protein synthesis was given right after the reminder, and the animals lost much of their fear, as though the memory had to be rebuilt, or reconsolidated, each time it was recalled.
The implications were unsettling. If recall opens a memory to revision, remembering is less like consulting an archive than like amending a manuscript. Every act of recall then furnishes an opportunity for distortion. This may help explain a puzzling habit of eyewitnesses: the more often they rehearse their testimony, the more confident they grow, but not the more accurate.
Doctors, however, saw a more (B) ____ prospect. Trials have tested giving patients with post-traumatic stress disorder a drug such as propranolol during an account of their ordeal. The hope is to blunt the memory's emotional sting without erasing the events themselves. The results so far have been mixed, and ethicists also warn of the possible misuse of a method able to soften painful memories.

Adults watching teenagers speed, dare one another or attempt reckless stunts often blame defiance or a simple lack of sense. Developmental scientists offer a more (A) ____ explanation. Brain regions linked to reward become highly responsive around puberty, but the networks supporting self-control keep maturing well into the twenties. For several years, then, the urge to seek thrills runs ahead of the capacity to restrain it, and no lecture on danger can simply close this gap between impulse and judgment.
The presence of friends widens the gap. In one well-known experiment, adolescents, young adults and older adults played a computer driving game, either alone or with peers watching from the same room. Teenagers took far more risks in front of an audience, whereas older adults behaved much the same in both conditions.
Such findings help explain the decision of every American state to (B) ____ some form of graduated licensing in law. New drivers gain full privileges in stages, and many states bar them from carrying young passengers during their first months behind the wheel. Studies have linked these rules to fewer crashes among young drivers. Researchers stress the modest aim of such rules. The point is not to isolate teenagers from their friends but to postpone the riskiest combinations until the brain's brakes have caught up with its accelerator.

For most of the past century, a unit of electricity cost a household the same whether it was used at noon or at midnight. That flat price was always something of a fiction. The cost of generating power fluctuates sharply over the day, and utilities must keep expensive standby plants ready for the evening peak, when people return home and switch on ovens, heaters and televisions. With the spread of smart meters, a growing number of utilities now offer time-of-use tariffs, charging more during peak hours and less when demand is (A) ____.
The rationale has grown more compelling with the rising share of solar and wind in the electricity supply. Their output is plentiful at some hours and meager at others. Nudging consumption toward sunny afternoons or windy nights therefore helps the grid absorb green power that might otherwise be squandered. Households with electric cars or heat pumps can (B) ____ considerable savings by scheduling charging and heating for cheaper periods.
Critics caution, however, that not every family can rearrange its day. Shift workers, the elderly and people caring for infants may have scant flexibility, and without safeguards they could end up paying more than they did under a flat rate. Some regulators have consequently insisted on keeping the new tariffs optional rather than mandatory.

Cement and steel together produce a large share of the world's carbon emissions, by many estimates more than a tenth, a fact that has sent architects in search of humbler materials. One of the most (A) ____ candidates grows in the dark. Mycelium, the threadlike root network of fungi, can be cultivated on agricultural detritus such as corn stalks or sawdust. Within days the filaments bind the loose material into a dense mass. The mass is then packed into molds and baked to arrest further growth, producing light bricks, sound-absorbing panels or insulation.
The appeal is clear: the material needs little energy to produce and sequesters carbon. At the end of its life, it can be turned into compost rather than consigned to a landfill. In 2014 a temporary tower built from such bricks stood in the courtyard of a New York art museum, and after the exhibition closed, the structure was taken apart and its bricks were composted.
Critics point out that these fungal bricks remain weak under pressure and easily damaged by moisture. For now, these flaws limit them to walls and panels carrying no weight. Researchers are testing coatings and mixed materials to remedy these deficiencies, but few expect fungal bricks to supplant concrete in skyscrapers anytime soon.

Why do audiences willingly sit through spectacles of anguish? Aristotle offered an answer in the Poetics that has lasted remarkably well. Tragedy, he wrote, stirs up pity and fear in order to bring about the catharsis of such emotions. The term is frustratingly (A) ____: Aristotle never defined it, and scholars have wrangled over its meaning for centuries.
One venerable reading, borrowed from medicine, treats catharsis as cleansing: just as a doctor removes harmful fluids from the body, tragedy releases built-up emotion and leaves the audience calmer than before. A second reading, rooted in religious ritual, construes catharsis as purification, a refining of the feelings rather than their removal. A third, supported by several modern scholars, treats the process as mainly intellectual, a moment of clarity in which the audience grasps why the hero's fall was both terrible and inevitable.
Modern psychology complicates the cleansing view. Experiments on aggression have found that venting anger tends to increase it rather than reduce it. Emotions, it seems, are not simply drained by expression. Aristotle's defenders reply that watching a tragedy is not venting but reflection, and that this distance makes all the difference.

Teachers have long assumed that what feedback says matters more than how it is worded. A growing body of research suggests otherwise. In one widely cited experiment, seventh graders got back essays marked with the same suggestions for revision. Half of the essays, chosen at random, also carried a short handwritten note from the teacher describing the comments as a mark of high standards and of faith in the student's ability to meet them. Students receiving the note were markedly more likely to revise their work, and the effect was especially pronounced among Black students, who had reported greater distrust of their school.
Psychologists explain the result in terms of trust. Framed as an expression of confidence, criticism otherwise read as a sign of a teacher's bias or disdain becomes an invitation to improve. Other studies suggest that feedback ranking students against their classmates can lower the motivation of all but the top performers. Some of these findings, however, have been hard to repeat.
None of this means that criticism should be diluted. The most efficacious feedback, researchers argue, is both honest and caring. It points out weaknesses clearly while making it plain that the teacher believes the student can fix them.

Family doctors have long recognized that many patients in their crowded waiting rooms suffer less from disease than from loneliness, debt or idleness, afflictions no pill can [A] ____. Social prescribing is an endeavor to redress them directly. Instead of medication or alongside it, a doctor refers the patient to a 'link worker', who helps the person find activities such as gardening groups, choirs, volunteering or walking clubs.
England has embraced the idea with particular enthusiasm. In 2019 the National Health Service pledged to fund link workers in general practices across the country, and the role has since become a fixture of primary care. Advocates contend that the approach treats the social roots of ill health rather than merely its symptoms. Anecdotes of isolated pensioners rediscovering a sense of purpose are abundant.
The evidence, however, remains [B] ____. Many evaluations are modest in scale, lack control groups, or rely on participants' own accounts of how they feel. It is therefore difficult to ascertain whether improvements stem from the activities themselves or would have occurred anyway. Researchers do not claim the idea is misguided. They argue instead for rigorous trials of a policy rolled out so widely, to establish which patients benefit and by how much.

When students practise mathematics, textbooks usually present problems in blocks: a dozen questions on one type of calculation, then a dozen on the next. The arrangement feels efficient, because by the third or fourth problem the method has become [A] ____ and answers come quickly. Yet a burgeoning body of research intimates that this smoothness is illusory.
In studies of so-called interleaved practice, learners tackle a mixture of problem types in an unpredictable order. Their performance during practice is typically inferior, since they must first discern which method a problem requires before applying it. On tests given days or weeks later, however, interleaved learners often outperform those who practised in blocks, occasionally by a considerable margin. Psychologists attribute the advantage to discrimination. Blocked practice lets students execute a procedure without ever deciding on its suitability, yet such judgment is precisely the skill an examination demands.
The finding poses a quandary for teachers and students alike. Interleaving feels more arduous, so learners routinely judge it less effective even after it has helped them, mistaking fluency for mastery. Publishers, for their part, have been sluggish in overhauling their exercises, and blocked practice remains entrenched in most classrooms.

Why do some teams learn from their mistakes while others conceal them? In the 1990s the Harvard researcher Amy Edmondson stumbled on a conundrum in scrutinizing hospital nursing units: the teams with the best leadership and relationships appeared to record more medication errors, not fewer. On closer inspection, they were not making more mistakes; they were simply more willing to [A] ____ them.
Edmondson called the underlying condition psychological safety, a shared belief in the safety of interpersonal risk-taking within a team. Such risk-taking encompasses admitting an error, asking a naive question or challenging a superior. Where it is absent, people stay silent to safeguard their reputations, and problems that could have been corrected early are left to [B] ____. The concept gained wide currency through Google's study of its own teams, known as Project Aristotle. The study found psychological safety more important to team effectiveness than any other factor it examined.
Edmondson is scrupulous in clarifying what the term does not mean. It is not a license for laxity or a promise of universal amiability. High standards and candid disagreement are compatible with it and, indeed, depend on it. A comfortable but unaccountable team, she warns, has merely settled into a comfort zone.

For decades hearing loss in old age was dismissed as a mere nuisance, a matter of raised voices and repeated sentences. That view is eroding. In 2024 the Lancet Commission on dementia prevention identified hearing loss as one of fourteen modifiable risk factors that together may account for nearly half of dementia cases worldwide. Why the link exists is still disputed. The strain of deciphering muffled sound may deplete mental resources, and people who cannot follow conversations often retreat into seclusion, forsaking the social life conducive to an active mind.
Yet many prospective beneficiaries of hearing aids are [A] ____ to acquire them, deterred by cost, inconvenience or the stigma of appearing decrepit. In 2022 the United States began allowing adults with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss to buy hearing aids over the counter, without a medical examination or prescription. The change was intended to curb prices and broaden access.
Whether hearing aids actually prevent dementia, however, remains uncertain. A large American trial published in 2023 found no slowing of cognitive decline from a hearing intervention across the study population as a whole. It did appear to help a subgroup of older adults already at higher risk. Researchers therefore counsel caution: treating hearing loss is worthwhile in its own right, but it should not be marketed as a guaranteed shield against dementia.

Open almost any score from the Baroque era and you will find a single bass line beneath the melody, marked with tiny numbers. This is the basso continuo, or 'continuous bass', the harmonic foundation of nearly all music from roughly 1600 to 1750. The numbers, called figures, did not spell out every note. They merely indicated the intervals to be sounded above the bass, leaving the keyboard player to [A] ____ the full chords on the spot.
This system made the continuo player something between an accompanist and a partner of the composer. An adept player was expected to read the figures fluently and to embellish them with tasteful ornaments, adapting the texture to the size of the room and the temperament of the soloist. No two performances were identical, so a Baroque work was never as fixed as a modern printed score implies.
The practice waned once composers began to write out accompaniments in full, a shift attesting to a growing desire to control every detail of performance. Early-music groups have since revived the practice. Historians caution, however, that our knowledge of continuo players' actual practice remains fragmentary, drawn from instruction manuals rather than recordings.

Fair-trade certification rests on a simple bargain. In exchange for meeting labor and environmental standards, cooperatives of small farmers receive a guaranteed minimum price for their coffee, plus a premium to invest in schools, clinics and equipment. In a slump, the floor shields growers from ruin; for washed Arabica beans it was raised in 2023 to $1.80 a pound.
The system's champions say it has given millions of farmers a [A] ____ against volatility. Its detractors are less sanguine. Only a fraction of certified coffee is actually sold on fair-trade terms, because demand from roasters lags behind supply. The remainder fetches ordinary market prices, even though the farmers have already paid the cost of certification. Some economists further argue that a price floor can trap small farmers in a crop of meager long-term prospects.
The commodity boom of the mid-2020s underscored a further irony. Droughts in Brazil and Vietnam drove coffee prices to record highs, with Arabica futures exceeding four dollars a pound in early 2025, and the guaranteed minimum became largely irrelevant. Yet many farmers gained only a small share of the windfall: they had sold their harvests in advance at lower prices, and intermediaries pocketed much of the profit.

Few pieces of self-help advice have proved more durable than the gratitude journal. The premise is very simple: once a week or even nightly, you write down a handful of things you are thankful for, and your mood will gradually brighten over the following months. Early studies seemed to support the practice with encouraging results. Participants who counted their blessings reported feeling more optimistic about the weeks ahead, and they even slept better than those who listed their daily problems.
Yet independent teams later tried to reproduce these findings with larger and more varied groups of people. The results proved less (A) ____. A gratitude exercise did tend to lift well-being, but the gains were modest and often disappeared when the comparison group did some other pleasant activity. Recalling a recent kindness or simply planning the week ahead produced similar gains. In other words, much of the benefit may come not from gratitude itself but from any structured pause for (B) ____.
None of this makes the journal worthless. Researchers note that the practice is cheap, harmless and genuinely comforting for some people. What the replications debunk is an inflated claim common in many wellness apps, namely that a few grateful sentences can transform a life. The more reasonable conclusion is that gratitude is one modest ingredient of a good life, not a cure-all.

Plunging into icy water after exercise has become a fixture of elite sport, and it is increasingly common on social media, where athletes and influencers extol the ritual for speeding recovery. The appeal is intuitive. Cold constricts blood vessels and dulls pain in tired muscles, so a few minutes in a tub of ice water ought to reduce the soreness and swelling that follow hard training.
The evidence, however, is more (A) ____ than the enthusiasm suggests. Reviews of controlled trials indicate that cold-water immersion can modestly reduce perceived soreness for a day or two after strenuous exercise. This may matter to athletes who must compete again quickly. Yet several studies have found a hidden cost in regular immersion after strength training. It may blunt the very adaptations the training is meant to produce, and over the following weeks regular bathers gained less muscle size and strength than their peers.
The likely explanation lies in inflammation. Athletes try to suppress it, but it is not merely a nuisance; it is part of the signal that prompts muscles to repair and grow. Researchers therefore suggest a pragmatic middle course. Athletes should reserve the ice bath for crowded competition schedules, when quick recovery is paramount, and skip it during periods devoted to building strength. For most recreational exercisers, the chief benefit may simply be that the plunge feels invigorating.

In almost every school system, children start school in cohorts defined by a single cutoff date. A child born the day after the cutoff may therefore be nearly a year older than a classmate born the day before it. At five or six, a year is an enormous share of a life. The oldest children in a class tend to be taller, more articulate and more emotionally mature than the youngest.
Teachers understandably notice these differences in their daily work. Studies in many countries have found that the youngest pupils in a cohort score lower on tests in the early grades and are more likely to be placed in remedial groups. Several studies have also reported higher rates of attention disorder diagnoses among them, raising the worry that ordinary immaturity is sometimes mistaken for a medical condition.
The gap in test scores generally narrows with age, but it rarely vanishes entirely. One reason is that early judgments can (A) ____ later opportunities, including placement in advanced classes. Some parents respond by delaying their child's entry by a year, a practice more common among affluent families. Researchers have proposed remedies that do not depend on family resources. One is to adjust test results for a child's age in months, so the youngest pupils would be compared with peers of the same age rather than simply with their classmates.

In May 2025, after more than three years of often fractious negotiation, member states of the World Health Organization adopted the Pandemic Agreement at the World Health Assembly in Geneva. The treaty was conceived in the aftermath of COVID-19, when wealthy countries secured vaccines long before poorer ones. It aims to make the global response to the next pandemic faster and more equitable.
The agreement calls for stronger surveillance of outbreaks around the world and promotes technology transfer to help developing countries manufacture vaccines and medicines. Under another provision, participating manufacturers would set aside a share of their production for the WHO to distribute during a pandemic. Crucially, the text affirms that the WHO has no authority to impose lockdowns, vaccine mandates or travel bans on sovereign states. This clause was added partly to (A) ____ critics who feared a loss of national control.
The treaty is not yet in force. It cannot open for signature until negotiators finish an annex governing how countries share samples of dangerous pathogens and the benefits derived from them, including vaccines. This annex has proved the most contentious issue of all. The treaty must then be ratified by sixty countries. The United States had announced its withdrawal from the WHO earlier that year and took no part in the adoption.

Each year the world manufactures more than 400 million tonnes of plastic, much of it used only once before it is thrown away. Most conventional plastics are made from petroleum and can persist in the environment for centuries, breaking into ever smaller particles rather than decomposing. Against this background, seaweed has emerged as an unlikely (A) ____ for alternative packaging.
Its appeal is easy to see. Seaweed grows quickly without fresh water, fertilizer or farmland, and growing it may even help absorb excess nutrients from coastal waters. Extracts like alginate can be cast into thin films or edible pods. One London start-up has supplied marathon organizers with drink capsules made this way, and runners can swallow them whole or throw them away because the skins will biodegrade within weeks.
Nevertheless, supporters admit that the obstacles are considerable. Seaweed films are often brittle or (B) ____, disintegrating on contact with moisture, which limits their use for liquids or in humid climates. Production costs remain several times higher than those of conventional plastic. Farming seaweed on a large scale could also harm marine ecosystems if poorly managed. Seaweed packaging is thus unlikely to replace petroleum-based plastics entirely; its more plausible role lies in niche uses like sachets and food wrappers, where rapid breakdown is an asset rather than a flaw.

For generations, the popular image of the medieval scriptorium was an entirely male one: monks bent over parchment, copying scripture by candlelight. Because most manuscripts are unsigned, scholars tended to assume that any anonymous hand belonged to a man. That assumption is now being (A) ____ by a growing body of evidence.
Some of it comes from the books themselves. A few women left colophons, terse notes at the end of a manuscript naming the copyist. One twelfth-century nun named Guda even drew a tiny self-portrait inside a decorated capital letter, with a line stating that she had written and painted the book herself. Experts on old handwriting have also traced whole groups of early manuscripts to communities of nuns, including the convent at Chelles near Paris.
More startling evidence emerged in 2019, when researchers examining the teeth of a woman buried at a German religious community roughly a thousand years ago found tiny bits of lapis lazuli in her dental plaque. Lapis lazuli was a costly blue pigment. The most plausible explanation is that she often licked the tip of her brush while painting manuscripts. This task was given only to highly skilled artists. Her case suggests that women's contribution to medieval book production was not minor but substantial, merely hidden by the custom of anonymity.
